items.readable_text:
Content:
The scalar triple product of three vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a},] [MATH: \mathbf{b},] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}] is defined as [MATH: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}).]

Content:
For example, suppose we have three vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a} = \langle -1,2,1 \rangle,] [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \langle 1,1,-2 \rangle,] and [MATH: \mathbf{c} = \langle 0,3,1 \rangle.] Let's compute their scalar triple product, [MATH: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}).]

Content:
First, we find the cross product:

Content:
[MATH: b × c|=|i|j|k; b_{1}|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{2}|c_{3}|; =|i|j|k; 1|1|− 2; 0|3|1|; =|1|− 2; 3|1|i −|1|− 2; 0|1|j +|1|1; 0|3|k; = (1 ⋅ 1 − (− 2) ⋅ 3)i − (1 ⋅ 1 − (− 2) ⋅ 0)j + (1 ⋅ 3 − 1 ⋅ 0)k; = 7i − j + 3k; = ⟨7, − 1, 3⟩]

Content:
Now, we can compute the scalar triple product:

Content:
[MATH: a ⋅ (b × c)|= ⟨ − 1, 2, 1⟩ ⋅ ⟨7, − 1, 3⟩; = (− 1) ⋅ 7 + 2 ⋅ (− 1) + 1 ⋅ 3; = − 6]

Content:
Note: The scalar triple product takes its name from the fact that it multiplies three vectors together and always results in a scalar.

Content:
Later, we will learn some geometric intuition behind the scalar triple product. But for now, we will focus on computing the scalar triple product.

The scalar triple product has two important properties.

Content:
First, scalars can be factored out of the product. For example,
[MATH: ({\color{red}2}\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{a} \cdot ({\color{red}2}\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times {\color{red}2}\mathbf{c}) = {\color{red}2}\left[ \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})\right].]

Content:
Second, if we swap exactly two vectors in the scalar triple product, the result changes sign. For example, swapping [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b},] we have
[MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{a}} \cdot ( {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}} \times \mathbf{c}) = - {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}} \cdot ( {\color{red}\mathbf{a}} \times \mathbf{c}).]

Content:
Note that if we swap twice, then the result remains the same, because the negatives cancel out. For example, swapping [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{b}] and then swapping [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{c},] we get

Content:

Content:
We have been using the fact for three vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a} = \langle a_1,a_2,a_3 \rangle,] [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \langle b_1,b_2,b_3 \rangle,] and [MATH: \mathbf{c} = \langle c_1,c_2,c_3 \rangle,] the scalar triple product can be computed as

Content:
[MATH: a ⋅ (b × c) =|a_{1}|a_{2}|a_{3}; b_{1}|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{2}|c_{3}|.]

Content:
But why is this true? To understand where this result comes from, first notice that in the formula for the triple product, the cross product can be expressed as follows:

Content:
[MATH: b × c|=|i|j|k; b_{1}|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{2}|c_{3}|; =|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{2}|c_{3}|i −|b_{1}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{3}|j +|b_{1}|b_{2}; c_{1}|c_{2}|k]

Content:
Now, when we take the dot product with [MATH: \mathbf{a},] we get an expression that is just the cofactor expansion across the first row of the matrix:

Content:
[MATH: a ⋅ (b × c)|= (a_{1}i + a_{2}j + a_{3}k) ⋅ (|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{2}|c_{3}|i −|b_{1}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{3}|j +|b_{1}|b_{2}; c_{1}|c_{2}|k); = a_{1}|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{2}|c_{3}|− a_{2}|b_{1}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{3}|+ a_{3}|b_{1}|b_{2}; c_{1}|c_{2}|; =|a_{1}|a_{2}|a_{3}; b_{1}|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{2}|c_{3}|]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The scalar triple product of three vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a},] [MATH: \mathbf{b},] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}] is defined as [MATH: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}).]

Content:
For example, suppose we have three vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a} = \langle -1,2,1 \rangle,] [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \langle 1,1,-2 \rangle,] and [MATH: \mathbf{c} = \langle 0,3,1 \rangle.] Let's compute their scalar triple product, [MATH: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}).]

Content:
First, we find the cross product:

Content:
[MATH: b × c|=|i|j|k; b_{1}|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{2}|c_{3}|; =|i|j|k; 1|1|− 2; 0|3|1|; =|1|− 2; 3|1|i −|1|− 2; 0|1|j +|1|1; 0|3|k; = (1 ⋅ 1 − (− 2) ⋅ 3)i − (1 ⋅ 1 − (− 2) ⋅ 0)j + (1 ⋅ 3 − 1 ⋅ 0)k; = 7i − j + 3k; = ⟨7, − 1, 3⟩]

Content:
Now, we can compute the scalar triple product:

Content:
[MATH: a ⋅ (b × c)|= ⟨ − 1, 2, 1⟩ ⋅ ⟨7, − 1, 3⟩; = (− 1) ⋅ 7 + 2 ⋅ (− 1) + 1 ⋅ 3; = − 6]

Content:
Note: The scalar triple product takes its name from the fact that it multiplies three vectors together and always results in a scalar.

Content:
Later, we will learn some geometric intuition behind the scalar triple product. But for now, we will focus on computing the scalar triple product.

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Scalar Triple Product Using the Definition

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{a}=\langle 2,-3,2 \rangle,] [MATH: \mathbf{b}=\langle -1,0,5 \rangle,] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}=\langle 1,2,3 \rangle.] Find [MATH: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we find the cross product:

[MATH: b × c|=|i|j|k; − 1|0|5; 1|2|3|; =|0|5; 2|3|i −|− 1|5; 1|3|j +|− 1|0; 1|2|k; = (0 ⋅ 3 − 5 ⋅ 2)i − (− 1 ⋅ 3 − 5 ⋅ 1)j + (− 1 ⋅ 2 − 0 ⋅ 2)k; = − 10i + 8j − 2k; = ⟨ − 10, 8, − 2⟩]

Now, we can compute the scalar triple product:

[MATH: a ⋅ (b × c)|= ⟨2, − 3, 2⟩ ⋅ ⟨ − 10, 8, − 2⟩; = 2 ⋅ (− 10) + (− 3) ⋅ 8 + 2 ⋅ (− 2); = − 48]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Calculating the Scalar Triple Product Using a Determinant

Content:
It turns out that the scalar triple product [MATH: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})] is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by [MATH: \mathbf{a},] [MATH: \mathbf{b},] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}.]

Content:
That is to say, if [MATH: \mathbf{a} = \langle a_1,a_2,a_3 \rangle,] [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \langle b_1,b_2,b_3 \rangle,] and [MATH: \mathbf{c} = \langle c_1,c_2,c_3 \rangle,] then

Content:
[MATH: a ⋅ (b × c) =|a_{1}|a_{2}|a_{3}; b_{1}|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{2}|c_{3}|.]

Content:
A proof of this result will be given at the end of the lesson. But for now, let's focus on computing the scalar triple product using the determinant above.

---

Item 6 — Example: Calculating the Scalar Triple Product Using a Determinant

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: \mathbf{a}=\langle 4,2,-1 \rangle,] [MATH: \mathbf{b}=\langle 0,2,1 \rangle,] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}=\langle -1,-1,2 \rangle.] Find [MATH: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Remember that the scalar triple product [MATH: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})] is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by [MATH: \mathbf{a},] [MATH: \mathbf{b},] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}.]

So, we have

[MATH: a ⋅ (b × c)|=|4|2|− 1; 0|2|1; − 1|− 1|2|; = 4 ⋅|2|1; − 1|2|− 2 ⋅|0|1; − 1|2|+ (− 1) ⋅|0|2; − 1|− 1|; = 4 ⋅ (2 ⋅ 2 − 1 ⋅ (− 1)) − 2 ⋅ (0 ⋅ 2 − 1 ⋅ (− 1)) + (− 1) ⋅ (0 ⋅ (− 1) − 2 ⋅ (− 1)); = 20 − 2 − 2; = 16.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Properties of the Scalar Triple Product

Content:
The scalar triple product has two important properties.

Content:
First, scalars can be factored out of the product. For example,
[MATH: ({\color{red}2}\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{a} \cdot ({\color{red}2}\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times {\color{red}2}\mathbf{c}) = {\color{red}2}\left[ \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})\right].]

Content:
Second, if we swap exactly two vectors in the scalar triple product, the result changes sign. For example, swapping [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b},] we have
[MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{a}} \cdot ( {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}} \times \mathbf{c}) = - {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}} \cdot ( {\color{red}\mathbf{a}} \times \mathbf{c}).]

Content:
Note that if we swap twice, then the result remains the same, because the negatives cancel out. For example, swapping [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{b}] and then swapping [MATH: \color{red}\mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{c},] we get

Content:
[MATH: a ⋅ (b × c)|= − b ⋅ (a × c); = − (− b ⋅ (c × a)); = b ⋅ (c × a).]

Content:
These properties arise naturally from the fact that the scalar triple product can be computed as a determinant.

Content:
1. If we multiply a row of the matrix by a number, then the determinant is multiplied by that number:
[MATH: |2a_{1}|2a_{2}|2a_{3}; b_{1}|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{2}|c_{3}|]
2. If we swap two rows, then the determinant changes sign:
[MATH: |a_{1}|a_{2}|a_{3}; b_{1}|b_{2}|b_{3}; c_{1}|c_{2}|c_{3}|]

Item 10 — Example: Calculating Scalar Triple Products Using Its Properties

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: \mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}),] if [MATH: 2\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times 3\mathbf{c}) = 5.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we factor out the constants and get

[MATH: 2a ⋅ (b × 3c)|= 5; 2 ⋅ [a ⋅ (b × 3c)]|= 5; 2 ⋅ 3 ⋅ [a ⋅ (b × c)]|= 5; a ⋅ (b × c)|= (5)/(6).]

Then, we swap [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{c}] to get

[MATH: c ⋅ (b × a)|= − (5)/(6),]

and again we swap [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] to get

[MATH: c ⋅ (a × b)|= (5)/(6).]

We have been using the fact for three vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a} = \langle a_1,a_2,a_3 \rangle,] [MATH: \mathbf{b} = \langle b_1,b_2,b_3 \rangle,] and [MATH: \mathbf{c} = \langle c_1,c_2,c_3 \rangle,] the scalar triple product can be computed as
